Currently Go race checker [https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector|https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector|smart-link]  is used only for detecting data races while running unit tests. The checker can be compiled with the binary to detect also at runtime. 


The outcome of this task is:
An automated way to gather detected races from race checker from all Kuadrant components running on Openshift cluster while/after testsuite runs.

Intern learning tasks:

* What components are there and how they run? Do they all use Go? Controllers vs Operands
* How to run testsuite, what it does 
** [https://github.com/Kuadrant/testsuite|https://github.com/Kuadrant/testsuite]
* How is Kuadrant/RHCL installed on cluster, what is OLM
** [https://github.com/Kuadrant/helm-charts-olm|https://github.com/Kuadrant/helm-charts-olm]
* How is Kuadrant and all components compiled? Compile with race checker and try manually
* Figure out automated way of collecting the data race detections
* Incorporate the test to testing pipeline (if needed as separate task)
** [https://github.com/Kuadrant/testsuite-pipelines|https://github.com/Kuadrant/testsuite-pipelines]

Consolidate known limitations across all egress capabilities into a single reference section. Review all egress user guides for consistency, accuracy, and completeness before the TP release.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* [ ] Write a consolidated known-limitations section covering all egress TP capabilities:
** Observability: metrics, access logging, distributed tracing limitations
** TokenRateLimitPolicy: streaming responses, API format support
** TelemetryPolicy: CEL expression limitations in egress context
** General: Istio-only support, user-configured egress gateway requirement, no Envoy Gateway support
* [ ] Review all egress user guides for:
** Consistent terminology and structure
** Accurate cross-references between guides
** TP designation present in all guides
** No stale references to developer preview
* [ ] Verify all guides are published and accessible on [docs.kuadrant.io|http://docs.kuadrant.io] and downstream RHCL docs

h2. Description

Validate that TokenRateLimitPolicy works on an Istio egress gateway and produce a user guide with a worked AI inference example. This follows the same validation pattern as AuthPolicy and RateLimitPolicy in 1.4 — those policies worked on egress without code changes, and TRLP uses the same wasm-shim/Limitador mechanism.

h3. What we expect

TokenRateLimitPolicy uses the same wasm-shim and Limitador infrastructure as RateLimitPolicy. Since RateLimitPolicy was validated on egress in 1.4 without code changes, TRLP should work the same way. The key difference is that TRLP extracts token counts from response bodies (e.g., OpenAI {{usage.total_tokens}}) rather than counting requests.

h3. Key things to validate

* TRLP attached to an egress gateway is picked up by the topology builder and reconciled correctly
* Token extraction from AI API responses works through TLS-originating egress (the egress gateway terminates internal mTLS and originates a new TLS connection to the external service — response body must still be accessible for token counting)
* Per-workload and per-tier token limits using workload identity (same SA-based identity as validated for RateLimitPolicy in 1.4)

h3. Potential risks

* TLS origination at the egress gateway could affect response body access for token extraction
* If the external AI API uses streaming responses (SSE), token extraction may behave differently

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* [ ] Validate TRLP enforces token-based rate limits on egress traffic to an AI-compatible API (or mock)
* [ ] Validate per-workload and per-tier token limits work with workload identity
* [ ] Document any limitations with streaming responses or specific API formats
* [ ] Write user guide with a worked AI inference example

h2. Description

Validate that Kuadrant's existing tracing infrastructure works correctly on egress gateways and document the findings by extending the observability guide with a tracing section.

h3. What we already have (from research)

*Wasm-shim trace propagation is implemented.* Envoy does not natively propagate trace context through wasm filters ([envoyproxy/envoy#22028|https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/issues/22028]), but the wasm-shim team solved this in [wasm-shim#47|https://github.com/Kuadrant/wasm-shim/issues/47] / [wasm-shim#48|https://github.com/Kuadrant/wasm-shim/issues/48]. The shim extracts {{traceparent}}/{{tracestate}}/{{baggage}} headers, creates child spans, and re-injects them into outgoing gRPC calls. It produces its own spans ({{kuadrant_filter}}, {{auth}}, {{ratelimit}}, etc.).

*Authorino ext_authz tracing works out of the box.* Envoy automatically creates a child span for ext_authz calls and propagates trace context via gRPC metadata. Authorino has built-in OTEL support — it receives {{traceparent}}, emits its own {{Check}} spans, and exports via OTLP. Configuration is via {{spec.tracing}} in Authorino CR or centrally via {{spec.observability.tracing}} in the Kuadrant CR.

*Tracing cluster reconciler should be gateway-agnostic.* The Istio tracing cluster reconciler ({{internal/controller/istio_tracing_cluster_reconciler.go}}) targets all Istio gateways with effective policies. This should include egress gateways — needs verification.

*OTEL setup on OpenShift requires:*

* Tempo Operator (trace backend, requires object storage: S3/MinIO/ODF)
* Red Hat build of OpenTelemetry Operator ({{OpenTelemetryCollector}} CR)
* Cluster Observability Operator (optional, enables Traces UI in OCP console)
* Istio {{Telemetry}} resource pointing to the OTEL collector

*Expected spans for the egress path (~6-8):*

# Workload sidecar outbound span
# Egress gateway inbound span
# Wasm-shim {{kuadrant_filter}} span
# Wasm-shim {{auth}} + {{auth_request}} sub-spans
# Authorino {{Check}} span
# Wasm-shim {{ratelimit}} sub-spans (if rate limiting active)
# Egress gateway outbound span to external service

h3. Key things to validate

* Tracing cluster reconciler picks up egress gateways (verify gateway selector logic)
* Span chain is complete and correct through the egress path
* {{disableContextPropagation: true}} in Istio Telemetry resource prevents trace headers leaking to external services (security consideration for egress)
* {{disableContextPropagation}} does not conflict with wasm-shim's manual header injection
* Trace context propagation works when workloads are NOT mesh-enrolled (no sidecar — reaching egress gateway via ClusterIP)

h3. Known limitations to document

||Limitation||Detail||
|Envoy wasm filters don't get trace context natively|Already mitigated by wasm-shim — document as resolved|
|{{disableContextPropagation}} stops trace at mesh boundary|By design — trace won't extend to external service|
|Trace header leaking to external services|Security concern — document {{disableContextPropagation}} as required for egress|
|No native proxy-wasm tracing API|wasm-shim works around this — cosmetic limitation only|
|B3 vs W3C format mismatch|Standardize on W3C (which Kuadrant already does)|

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* [ ] Verify existing tracing infrastructure (tracing cluster reconciler, wasm-shim spans, Authorino spans) works on egress gateways
* [ ] Validate span chain is complete across the egress path with policies attached
* [ ] Validate {{disableContextPropagation}} prevents trace headers reaching external services
* [ ] Extend observability guide with tracing section covering OTEL setup, expected spans, and egress-specific considerations

Add partial support for MCP Resources federation in the current stateful protocol version, scoped to unblocking MCP Apps (SEP-1865) UI rendering through the gateway.

h3. Context

Ecosystem Engineering (Daniele Martinoli, Ilan Pinto) are deploying hosted MCPs (Lightspeed/Insights MCP, Assisted Service MCP) to serve cloud agents (initially ChatGPT). These MCPs expose UI widgets via MCP Apps, which reference resources (ui:// URIs) in tool output metadata. Without resource federation, the gateway silently degrades tool output to raw text.

h3. Scope (partial support)

* Federation of resources/list and resources/read for upstream MCP servers
* URI prefix-in-path rewriting for ui:// resources to avoid collisions across upstream servers
* Rewriting of _meta.ui.resourceUri in tools/call responses so resource URIs resolve correctly through the gateway

h3. Out of scope

* Full resources federation (subscriptions, templates, non-ui:// schemes)
* Stateless (Streamable HTTP) protocol resources support (tracked separately under CONNLINK-1057)

h3. References

* GitHub issue: https://github.com/Kuadrant/mcp-gateway/issues/788
* MCP Apps SEP-1865: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/seps/1865-mcp-apps-interactive-user-interfaces-for-mcp
* Slack thread with Ecosystem Engineering: https://redhat-external.slack.com/archives/C093L6XMJLW/p1782405566891029

h2. Goal

As part of the parent epic (CONNLINK-1218) Two-Phase Release Process, implement the required RFC 0020: Two-Phase Release Workflow changes in the *helm-charts* repository.

Target repository: [https://github.com/kuadrant/helm-charts|https://github.com/kuadrant/helm-charts|smart-link] 

Adopt the epic's standard two-phase GitHub Actions release model so releases are auditable, policy-compliant, and resilient:

* *Phase 1 -- Prepare & Validate:* release changes happen via pull requests on release branches; CI validates the branch (tests, version checks, dependency checks); a human review gate (PR approval) separates code changes from artifact publication.
* *Phase 2 -- Publish:* after approval/merge, a dedicated workflow publishes artifacts (tags, GitHub Release, container images, etc.) without writing directly to protected branches.

Existing workflows and repository documentation should be used as the starting point to guide the necessary changes.

h2. Expected Deliverables

# *Add or update* {{release.yaml}} -- introduce the machine-readable release manifest at the repository root containing:
#* Component name and version (using {{0.0.0}} as the sentinel value on {{main}} to indicate "targets latest / under active development").
#* Dependencies on other Kuadrant components and their required released versions.
# *Implement Phase 1 workflow (Prepare & Validate)* -- add or update a GitHub Actions workflow that:
#* Creates or targets a release branch.
#* Opens a PR with version bumps, changelog updates, and any release-specific changes.
#* Runs CI validation (tests, version checks, dependency checks) on the release branch.
#* Enforces a human review gate before publication proceeds.
# *Implement Phase 2 workflow (Publish)* -- add or update a GitHub Actions workflow that:
#* Triggers after the Phase 1 PR is approved and merged.
#* Publishes artifacts (Git tags, GitHub Release, container images, etc.).
#* Is observable and isolated -- does not write directly to protected branches.
# *Wire up the version-gate CI check* -- add a CI check that consumes {{release.yaml}} to:
#* Verify that all declared component dependencies have published the required GitHub Releases before this component's release can proceed.
#* Block releases when upstream dependencies are not yet available.
# *Deprecate legacy release workflows* -- identify and remove or disable any existing single-phase release jobs that are superseded by the new two-phase model.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* A {{release.yaml}} file exists at the repository root and follows the schema defined in RFC 0020.
* The Phase 1 (Prepare & Validate) workflow runs successfully on release branches and enforces PR-based review before publication.
* The Phase 2 (Publish) workflow publishes all required artifacts only after Phase 1 approval/merge.
* No workflow writes directly to protected branches.
* The version-gate CI check correctly blocks releases when upstream dependencies have not yet published their required versions.
* Legacy single-phase release workflows are removed or disabled.
* All changes are consistent with the patterns and requirements described in RFC 0020 and the parent epic CONNLINK-1218.

h2. References

* Parent epic: CONNLINK-1218
* RFC: [RFC 0020: Two-Phase Release Workflow|https://github.com/Kuadrant/architecture/pull/178]
* Related audit/compliance work: [CONNLINK-896|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-896]

items.toString:
Implement *RFC 0020: Two-Phase Release Workflow* across all affected Kuadrant component repositories to make releases auditable, policy-compliant, and resilient.

This epic introduces a *standard two-phase GitHub Actions release model*:

* *Phase 1 – Prepare & Validate*
** Release changes happen via pull requests on release branches.
** CI validates the branch (tests, version checks, dependency checks).
** A *human review gate* (PR approval) separates code changes from artifact publication, satisfying Red Hat Segregation of Duties and branch protection requirements.

* *Phase 2 – Publish*

* After approval/merge, a dedicated workflow publishes artifacts (tags, GitHub Release, container images, etc.).
* Publishing is observable, isolated, and does not write directly to protected branches.

To support consistent automation across repositories with different build systems, each repo will add a {{release.yaml}} file as the *machine‑readable source of truth* for:

* Component name and version (including {{0.0.0}} as a sentinel “targets latest / under active development” on {{main}}).
* Dependencies on other Kuadrant components and their required released versions.

A *version‑gate CI check* will consume {{release.yaml}} to:

* Block operator releases until all operand dependencies have published the required GitHub Releases.
* Eliminate references to non‑existent images and reduce cross‑repo release failures.

h3. Why this work is needed

The *Kuadrant* *v1.5.0 release* exposed systemic issues with the existing single‑workflow release model, including:

* False success reporting and hidden chained workflows.
* Silent downstream failures when dependencies were not yet released.
* Policy violations from direct commits to protected branches.
* Lack of automated dependency gating between operators and operands.

In addition, internal audit and compliance requirements (see *CONNLINK-896*) mandate:

* Enforced *Segregation of Duties* (human review between code changes and publication).
* No direct writes to protected branches by automation.
* Traceable, self‑contained release workflows per repository.

This epic addresses both the technical reliability gaps identified in RFC 0020 and the audit/compliance concerns captured in [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-896|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-896|smart-link].

h3. Scope & follow‑up issues

This epic will track:

* Definition and rollout of the *two‑phase workflows* in GitHub Actions.
* Introduction and wiring of {{release.yaml}} and the version gate in each affected repo.
* Migration of existing release jobs to the new model.

*Follow‑up issues will be created per impacted repository* to:

* Add / update {{release.yaml}}.
* Implement or adjust the two‑phase workflows.
* Deprecate legacy single‑phase release jobs.

*References*

* RFC: *“RFC 0020: Two-Phase Release Workflow”*
[https://github.com/Kuadrant/architecture/pull/178|https://github.com/Kuadrant/architecture/pull/178|smart-link]
* Related audit / compliance work:
[https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-896|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-896|smart-link]

Currently, RHCL uses a single {{stable}} OLM channel. This creates two significant problems:

*Problem 1: Rewriting upgrade paths for backport patches*

Adding a patch release to an older minor version requires modifying existing bundle metadata to insert the new version into the upgrade graph. For example, with latest at {{1.3.2}}, the current upgrade path is:

{noformat}1.2.0 → 1.2.1 → 1.3.0 → 1.3.1 → 1.3.2{noformat}

Adding {{1.2.2}} requires rewriting an existing bundle's {{replaces}}/{{skipRange}} to produce:

{noformat}1.2.0 → 1.2.1 → 1.2.2 → 1.3.0 → 1.3.1 → 1.3.2{noformat}

This is error-prone and violates the expectation that published bundles are immutable.

*Problem 2: No way for customers to pin to a minor release*

Customers subscribed to {{stable}} receive all upgrades including minor version bumps. There is no supported way to enable automatic updates scoped to patch releases only.

h2. Why it Matters

Last year we rolled out a new lifecyle model for our operators [https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1GD29PRJwYckO6zw73fw3eVUu1hmsdMYhNuKxx4uX7SM/edit#slide=id.g1ccea862d8c_46_0|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1GD29PRJwYckO6zw73fw3eVUu1hmsdMYhNuKxx4uX7SM/edit#slide=id.g1ccea862d8c_46_0|smart-link]  which aims to standardize the channel naming scheme. Now we need means to enforce it.

Related: [Standard Channel Naming Scheme|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/KONFLUX-3671] 



*Proposed Solution*

Introduce per-minor OLM channels (e.g., {{stable-1.2}}, {{stable-1.3}}). Each channel only carries patch releases for that minor version. The {{stable}} channel would be marked as deprecated and eventually removed, once a migration strategy is agreed upon.

Benefits:

* New patch bundles for older minors can be appended to their own channel without touching any existing bundle.
* Customers can subscribe to a minor-specific channel and get automatic patch updates without being moved to a new minor version.

*Open Questions*

# *Customer migration*: How do we communicate to existing {{stable}} subscribers that they should migrate to a minor-specific channel or accept they will continue to receive minor upgrades?
# *Deprecation of* {{stable}}: Is there a supported mechanism in OpenShift Console / OLM to mark a channel as deprecated, surfacing a deprecation notice to cluster administrators? If so, this would be the first step before any removal. *[EDIT: it is very simple to add a deprecation message to a channel entry, here is the entry in the OLM docs:* [+*https://olm.operatorframework.io/docs/reference/file-based-catalogs/#olmdeprecations*+|https://olm.operatorframework.io/docs/reference/file-based-catalogs/#olmdeprecations]*]*
# *Removal of* {{stable}}: Can the {{stable}} channel be removed from a future catalog without disrupting clusters already subscribed to it? What is OLM's behavior when a subscribed channel disappears — does it block updates, error, or silently stop? *This needs to be answered before any removal decision is made.*

{quote}*Note:* Deprecation and eventual removal of {{stable}} is under consideration but not yet decided. The answers to the questions above will inform that decision.{quote}

*Acceptance Criteria*

* [ ] Per-minor channels exist (e.g., {{stable-1.2}}, {{stable-1.3}}, ...) alongside {{stable}}
* [ ] Adding a patch to an older minor requires only a new bundle entry in that minor's channel, no rewrites to existing bundles
* [ ] A customer subscribed to {{stable-1.N}} receives only {{1.N.x}} updates automatically
* [ ] Migration path from {{stable}} to minor channels is documented
* [ ] Decision on deprecation/removal of {{stable}} is reached and documented (out of scope for initial implementation)

Create and publish a custom dynamic plugin for Red Hat Connectivity Link (RHCL) that integrates into Red Hat Developer Hub (RHDH). h3. Summary

The upgrade pipeline should not clean up before the upgrade.

A {{make smoke}} runs before upgrading to the desired catalog version. Because of this, an issue was not caught before it was released to the public.

h3. Context

The current pipeline performs cleanup during the upgrade flow.

This creates a risk of missing similar issues in future upgrades.

h3. Acceptance criteria

* Add a flag that skips teardown when needed.
* Enable the flag in the pipeline.
* Prevent cleanup before the upgrade when the flag is used.

h3. Other information

* The issue was linked to [CONNLINK-1130|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-1130].
* The goal is to prevent similar scenarios in future upgrades.
items.toString:
h3. Summary

The upgrade test plan should include a live upgrade check.  
A complete end-to-end upgrade test currently ends with teardown, which leaves gaps in release validation.

h3. Context

The current pipeline performs cleanup during the upgrade flow.  
This creates a risk of missing similar issues in future upgrades.

An extra step is needed where the pipeline is paused and an authenticated rate limiting test is performed before the upgrade.  
The topology should no longer be cleared, because many customers do not clean up gateways between upgrades.

h3. Acceptance criteria

* Add a flag that skips teardown when needed: {{--no-teardown}}.
* Enable the flag in the pipeline.
* Prevent cleanup before the upgrade when the flag is used.
* Add a new pipeline phase called {{live-upgrade}}.
* In {{live-upgrade}}, run {{make testsuite/tests/singlecluster/test_rate_limit_authz.py --no-teardown}} before doing the upgrade.
* Keep the resources on the cluster until the whole suite finishes.
* Do another sanity check at the end to confirm the behavior is still working post upgrade.
* Then do a cleanup.

h3. Other information

The issue was linked to [CONNLINK-1130|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONNLINK-1130].  
The goal is to prevent similar scenarios in future upgrades.

As part of 1.4.0 we migrated the away from {{WasmPlugin}} to {{EnvoyFilter}} for our wasm configuration to configure {{allow_on_headers_stop_iteration}}, to move toward supporting request body processing. [https://github.com/Kuadrant/kuadrant-operator/pull/1953|https://github.com/Kuadrant/kuadrant-operator/pull/1953|smart-link] 

As part of this work we missed the cleanup of existing {{WasmPlugin}} objects. This would result in the envoy configuration potentially having two merged copies of the wasm config. The protection policy configuration for one of these would be snapshotted at the state at the time of upgrade, and the other would reflect current state.

A workaround to mitigate, the existing {{WasmPlugin}} objects in gateway namespaces, with the kuadrant ownership label should be removed, _once_ it’s been confirmed that the new {{EnvoyFilter}} is in place.

We need to implement upgrade logic in the operator, potentially through an initContainer or the reconcile process itself, to ensure we remove old {{WasmPlugin}} objects only once the {{EnvoyFilter}} is in place to ensure the upstream is always protected. It’s worth noting rolling back the PR would require the inverse cleanup to remove the new {{EnvoyFilter}}.

Yet to confirm, but there’s a chance that this duplication of the wasm-shim is the root cause of the OOM issue [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-68589|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-68589|smart-link]

_Description:_ To protect against Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL) attacks, where a quantum computer would be powerful enough in a near future to break current classical asymmetric cryptography, it is critical to enable the quantum-safe key encapsulation ML-KEM in your component/product.

As of OCP 4.22, the version of Go (1.25) provides ML-KEM for TLS endpoints, so the capability is available to you. It's now on your team to validate it.

_Action Required:_
* This was a release blocker for OpenShift 4.22 if you were platform aligned & should be supported no later than your first release after OCP 4.22 GA if you are not platform aligned
* An email reminder was sent on APR 30 about this work - Please test!

_Acceptance Criteria:_
* All local or hardcoded TLS configurations (protocols, ciphers, curves) have been removed from the solution codebase and deployment scripts
* Testing support toward OCP 4.22 - ensure all TLS endpoints are at least offering ML-KEM to clients during key exchange
* Discover all TLS ports in an OpenShift cluster and query each one to ensure it's offering ML-KEM
* Discover all TLS ports in a specific namespace and query each one to ensure it's offering ML-KEM
* Write dedicated functional tests within each component where necessary for short-lived TLS endpoints to ensure they're offering ML-KEM
* Use tls-scanner tool for verification (https://github.com/openshift/tls-scanner)

_Instructions:_
1. Review the testing approaches and choose appropriate strategy for your component

items.toString:
This is a clone of [PLMPGM-7881|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PLMPGM-7881].

*Description:*

To protect against Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL) attacks, where a quantum computer would be powerful enough in a near future to break current classical asymetric cryptography, it is critical to enable the quantum-safe key encapsulation ML-KEM in your component/product. 

As of OCP 4.22, the version of Go (1.25) provides ML-KEM for TLS endpoints, so the capability is available to you. It’s now on your team to validate it.

*Action Required:*

* {color:#ff5630}*This was a release blocker for OpenShift 4.22 if you were platform aligned & should be supported no later than your first release after OCP 4.22 GA if you are not platform aligned*{color}
* {color:#ff5630}*An email reminder was sent on APR 30 about this work - Please test!*{color}

If you have questions or need help, please contact [~accountid:70121:3adcdb0f-fb7f-4bd0-bff1-8be388f4d320] [~accountid:6397a089fbf54baf29035c6c], [~accountid:70121:cda96363-690c-4fe8-90a3-1d010e7202f5],  [~accountid:70121:461bf05d-2af3-4eca-af46-bcb519faef82], [~accountid:712020:6d7ad9a4-c4ec-4145-95fd-8f5641da08b4], or [~accountid:712020:aa20dad2-20d5-4b63-b70f-b8b66c05a619]  in [#forum-ocp-tls-strict-obedience|https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C098FU5MRAB].

NEED TO UPDATE SECTION.

*Acceptance Criteria (Definition of Done):*

* All local or hardcoded TLS configurations (protocols, ciphers, curves) have been removed from the solution codebase and deployment scripts
* *The biggest thing to reiterate over the last month is testing support toward OCP 4.22, which is to make sure all TLS endpoints are at least offering ML-KEM to clients during key exchange. Testing happens in three approaches.*
*# Discover all TLS ports in an OpenShift cluster and query each one to ensure it’s offering ML-KEM
*# Discover all TLS ports in a specific namespace and query each one to ensure it’s offering ML-KEM
*# Write dedicated functional tests within each component where necessary for short-lived TLS endpoints to ensure they’re offering ML-KEM
* The primary tool we have to verify PQC readiness is {{tls-scanner}} 
** Source code:[https://github.com/openshift/tls-scanner|https://github.com/openshift/tls-scanner|smart-link]
** OpenShift CI step definition:[https://steps.ci.openshift.org/reference/tls-scanner-run|https://steps.ci.openshift.org/reference/tls-scanner-run|smart-link] (use {{PQC_CHECK=true}})
* The first layer is essentially done by the {{tls-scanner}} periodic CI testing, but it only covers basic cluster installation and configuration. *Layered products should rely on the second approach, where they can point the* {{tls-scanner}} *at a namespace where they’ve installed their components for integration testing* ([example|https://github.com/openshift/release/pull/78651]). The third approach is necessary for short-lived endpoints (e.g., spinning up a server quickly and tearing it down during normal operations). The tls-scanner cannot guarantee that it will find these transient endpoints. So it’s up to the component teams to add testing for those cases using appropriate integration testing techniques that best suit their projects. For folks who remember the Rapid Reset patching we did a couple years ago, this will look similar (e.g., testing that asserts a given endpoint comes up with  HTTP1.1 instead of HTTP2).
* PQC and FIPS are mutually exclusive until everyone builds on UBI 10
* Customers must plan for TLS changes, with adequate maintenance windows (many components will restart as TLS setting updates roll through the cluster)
* The overall TLS adherence and PQC posture is documented consistently in a single place, as opposed to each team documenting the behavior separately in different parts of the OpenShift documentation (increasing the surface area for discrepancies in describing the behavior)

The {{tls-scanner}} is now being used in two different, opinionated jobs. [One uses it to assert PQC readiness|https://steps.ci.openshift.org/job?org=openshift&repo=tls-scanner&branch=main&test=tls13-pqc-readiness] (are these TLS endpoints at least offering ML-KEM?) for 4.22, and the [other uses it to validate TLS adherence|https://steps.ci.openshift.org/job?org=openshift&repo=tls-scanner&branch=main&test=tls13-adherence] is propagating through the cluster (are these TLS endpoints using the same TLS settings as the OpenShift API server?), which is important for OpenShift 5.0 goals.

Other reminders from various Slack and Jira discussions over the last month:

* Outbound TLS connections are not subject to this work
* [Christopher Alfonso|mailto:calfonso@redhat.com] and [Mike Worthington|mailto:mworthin@redhat.com] have been sending reminders in Jira regarding issues linked to the OpenShift 5.0 initiative - mainly for TLS consistency initiative
* Further restricting key exchange groups using TLS settings is an OpenShift 5.1 roadmap item
* Converting HTTP traffic to using HTTPS is technically out-of-scope for this work, but highly recommended that teams open tickets to track that gap and prioritize them as a good security practice
* The Golang community has [accepted|https://github.com/golang/go/issues/77626#issuecomment-4299122920] the proposed public crypto standard library API changes for ML-DSA – which will be important for future PQC work
* If you’re observing NO_TLS in your results, it could be related to the absence of {{--starttls}}, which is an optional argument to {{testssl.sh}} to detect connections that aren’t encrypted by default ([prototype for Postgres|https://github.com/openshift/tls-scanner/compare/main...vladbologa:tls-scanner:starttls-postgres-support]) - if this is impacts you, please weigh in on the [thread|https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/C098FU5MRAB/p1775820659660779]
* Reminder to use the [TLS Profile Compliance — Implementation Reference|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1NoHP2nZdg-xUkcB2y2BtI8469-iicdSG7xJwRad4kF0/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.p836qlye75wr]

As always, drop questions in [#forum-ocp-tls-strict-obedience|https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C098FU5MRAB] if you have them.

*Need Guidance?*

The team assembled a [technical guide|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cMc9E8psHfnoK06ntR8kHSWB8d3rMtmldhnmM4nImjs/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.ip4ox6ogxnl1] with general guidelines and code samples. Start there!
Also check the [Frequently asked questions|https://docs.google.com/document/d/11t7Q4teUQaHPCgtFoMwVsVrdYcvAW08Vrm5kHh8dYGM/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.s53z59b1pltc].

items.toString:
Add a GitHub Actions workflow to the mcp-gateway-product-build repo that automatically approves and merges pull requests from red-hat-konflux[bot] targeting the nightly branch ONLY. Currently, after Konflux builds complete, the nudge bot opens PRs to update the image digests in bundle-generation/image-pullspecs/, but these still require manual approval and merge. For the nightly pipeline to be fully hands-off, these should be auto-merged.

The workflow must:
- Only trigger on PRs targeting the nightly branch (not rhcl-1.x release branches)
- Only act on PRs from red-hat-konflux[bot] on konflux/component-updates/* branches
- Auto-approve and merge matching PRs
- Release branches must continue to require manual review and merge of nudge PRs
